research_brief.topic: TSMC — the semiconductor foundry that controls all advanced chip production
research_brief.research_summary: TSMC controls 65% of global foundry revenue and 90%+ of advanced-node manufacturing (3nm/2nm), with no viable alternative at volume until at least 2028. Every major AI accelerator, every frontier model training run, every NVIDIA GPU depends on a single industrial node concentrated in Taiwan — 160km from mainland China. The irreplaceability is structural: TSMC's 'one-hour ecosystem' of co-located suppliers took 30 years to build and cannot be transplanted. Governments are spending hundreds of billions to reduce this dependency, but TSMC's own founder says it's 'a very expensive exercise in futility.' The strongest animation approach is a progressive chokepoint-map build that narrows a global supply chain down to a single amber node — the visual structure mirrors the argument.

data_points.claim: TSMC holds ~65% of global foundry revenue and over 90% of advanced-node manufacturing (3nm/2nm). No other company can manufacture at leading-edge nodes at volume.
data_points.source_name: PatentPC / Counterpoint Research foundry market data
data_points.usable_as: hook and stat_card — the first number viewers see

data_points.claim: TSMC Q1 2026 revenue: $35.7 billion — 35.1% year-on-year increase, a new quarterly record. Full-year 2025 revenue: ~$122.9 billion, up 31.6% YoY.
data_points.source_name: TSMC Q1 2026 earnings report via Vucense
data_points.usable_as: stat_card — demonstrates that TSMC's leverage is strengthening, not weakening

data_points.claim: TSMC's CoWoS advanced packaging for AI chips is sold out through 2026. CoWoS capacity growing from 35K wafers/month in 2024 to projected 127K/month by end-2026 — and still insufficient to meet demand.
data_points.source_name: Fusion Worldwide: Inside the AI Bottleneck
data_points.usable_as: chokepoint-within-a-chokepoint — script anchor for 'there's a second gate inside the gate'

data_points.claim: TSMC Arizona currently represents less than 5% of leading-edge production. At current ramp rates, it won't materially reduce Taiwan dependence until 2028 or later.
data_points.source_name: CNBC / analyst estimates on TSMC Arizona capacity
data_points.usable_as: script_anchor — kills the 'CHIPS Act fixed it' misconception

data_points.claim: TSMC's 2nm yield is ~65%; Samsung's competing 2nm process yields ~30%. This yield gap explains why fabless companies cannot simply switch foundries — quality is not interchangeable.
data_points.usable_as: script_anchor — the mechanism behind irreplaceability; not just location, but 30 years of accumulated process yield

data_points.claim: TSMC founder Morris Chang said efforts to build TSMC's equivalent outside Taiwan are 'a very expensive exercise in futility.' The reason: TSMC's 'one-hour ecosystem' — every supplier, tool, and material within 1 hour — took 30 years to build and cannot be transplanted.
data_points.usable_as: closing_punch — the structural argument that the chokepoint is permanent on any 10-year horizon

data_points.claim: US CHIPS Act: $52 billion. EU Chips Act: €43 billion. Japan: ¥3.9 trillion in semiconductor subsidies. All three are fundamentally programs to reduce concentration at TSMC. None will deliver meaningful results before 2028.
data_points.usable_as: stat_card — shows the scale of the problem and how many governments it has mobilized

misconceptions.myth: The CHIPS Act solved the semiconductor concentration problem
misconceptions.reality: TSMC Arizona represents <5% of leading-edge production and won't change the dependency picture until 2028 at earliest.
misconceptions.source: CNBC analyst estimates, TSMC earnings calls

misconceptions.myth: Samsung and Intel are viable alternatives to TSMC at advanced nodes
misconceptions.reality: Samsung's 2nm yields ~30% vs TSMC's ~65%. Intel's 18A is at ~55% and primarily for internal use. At volume, there is no alternative for the most advanced chips.

misconceptions.myth: Chip companies like Apple and NVIDIA make their own chips
misconceptions.reality: They are fabless — they design chips but outsource all manufacturing. TSMC fabricates Apple's A-series, NVIDIA's H/B series, AMD's Ryzen/EPYC, Qualcomm's Snapdragon.
misconceptions.source: TSMC customer list, foundry model explanation

audience_insights.knowledge_level: Audience knows TSMC exists and is important. They do not understand the supply chain structure (fabless → EDA → foundry → OSAT), the yield-based moat, or why the Arizona fab doesn't change anything. The 'one-hour ecosystem' concept is almost entirely unknown to a general business/tech audience.
pain_points: Frustration that US/EU governments are spending massive sums but the problem appears unsolvable
Confusion about why chip manufacturing is so geographically concentrated when 'everything is digital'
Anxiety about AI supply chain vulnerability that nobody seems to have a clear answer for

angles_discovered.name: Why Everything Depends on One Factory
angles_discovered.hook: Every AI chip, every smartphone, every data center runs through one factory on a 36km² island. There is no backup.
angles_discovered.why_now: TSMC Q1 2026 record revenue ($35.7B, +35% YoY) and NVIDIA overtaking Apple as TSMC's largest customer signal that AI has made this concentration more acute, not less. The chokepoint is tightening.
grounded_in: 90%+ advanced node market share data point

angles_discovered.name: The Moat Is a Process, Not a Place
angles_discovered.hook: The US is spending $52 billion to build a fab. TSMC's founder says it won't work — and the reason has nothing to do with location.
angles_discovered.why_now: CHIPS Act is active, Arizona fab is running, yet the fundamental dependency hasn't moved. The yield-gap data (TSMC 65% vs Samsung 30% at 2nm) and the 'one-hour ecosystem' argument are the underserved explanation for why money alone can't solve this.
grounded_in: TSMC 2nm yield 65% vs Samsung 30% data point

angles_discovered.name: AI Hardware Has One Chokepoint
angles_discovered.hook: Every frontier AI model runs on hardware that passes through a single bottleneck. This is not a policy problem. It's a physics and economics problem.
angles_discovered.why_now: NVIDIA's rise to TSMC's #1 customer position in 2026, and CoWoS packaging being fully sold out through 2026, directly tie AI capability to TSMC capacity in a way that investors and operators can immediately feel.
grounded_in: NVIDIA overtaking Apple as TSMC largest customer
CoWoS sold out through 2026 data point
Q1 2026 revenue record driven by AI demand

visual_references.description: Progressive diagram build: supply chain shown as nodes building from left (fabless design) to right (consumer product), with a single amber-highlighted chokepoint node (TSMC) lighting up last
visual_references.what_works: The visual argument matches the verbal argument — the diagram literally narrows to one node. Viewers understand the leverage point before the narration finishes the sentence.

visual_references.description: Stat card with large numbers: '90% of advanced nodes' shown as a bar collapsing into TSMC's share, Samsung's 12% shown as a contrast sliver
visual_references.what_works: Bar chart with dramatic proportion difference is immediately readable. Works for both desktop and mobile.

visual_references.description: Chokepoint map: world map with arrows from Apple (Cupertino), NVIDIA (Santa Clara), AMD (Santa Clara), Qualcomm (San Diego) all converging on a single point in Hsinchu, Taiwan
visual_references.what_works: Geographic convergence makes the abstraction physical. Everyone understands a map.

metadata.animation_technique_notes: Progressive chokepoint-map build is the ideal technique for this topic. The visual structure of a supply chain diagram that narrows to one amber node mirrors the argument perfectly. HyperFrames (HTML/CSS/GSAP) is the preferred runtime for diagram evolution — vector nodes animating sequentially, arrows drawing, chokepoint lighting amber at the end of each sequence. No Manim needed (no math); no AI video needed for core argument (though a semiconductor wafer hero image would add production value at the cold open).
